Shavuot. The Feast of Weeks is a two-day festival occurring fifty days after Passover, typically in May or June. It commemorates the giving of the Torah at Mount Sinai, when God revealed the law to the Israelites, and also marks the spring harvest as one of the three pilgrimage festivals in Jewish tradition.

The name Shavuot literally means "weeks," referring to the seven-week counting period called the Omer between Passover and this festival. The holiday celebrates the receiving of the Torah and the Ten Commandments, making it a festival of Jewish law, learning, and covenant with God. All-night study sessions called Tikkun Leil Shavuot, which means "repairing the night of Shavuot," are traditionally held, during which Jews study texts from the entire Torah.

Dairy foods, especially cheesecake and blintzes, are traditionally eaten, with various mystical and practical reasons offered for this custom. The Book of Ruth is read during Shavuot, connecting themes of conversion, loyalty, and choosing to be part of the Jewish covenant community. Shavuot is unique among major Jewish holidays in having no specific ritual observances mandated by biblical law; its character as a Torah holiday develops through rabbinic tradition. The festival originally emphasized the barley and wheat harvest, but the spiritual significance shifted to focus on the giving of the Torah. In Israel, Shavuot is observed for one day; in the Diaspora, it is traditionally observed for two days. The central focus of the holiday celebrates Torah's revelation at Sinai, connected through the counting of the Omer period that links it to Passover, and remains central to Jewish identity as a tradition rooted in Torah study and observance.
